sections.heading: The legal rule
sections.body: 129. Whoever intentionally uses force to any person, without that person’s consent, in order to the committing of any offence, or intending by the use of such force to cause, or knowing it to be likely that by the use of such force he will cause injury, fear or annoyance to the person to whom the force is used, is said to use criminal force to that other

sections.heading: Essential ingredients
sections.body: Whoever intentionally uses force to any person, without that person’s consent, in order to the committing of any offence, or intending by the use of such force to cause, or knowing it to be likely that by the use of such force he will cause injury, fear or annoyance to the person to whom the force is used, is said to use criminal force to that other

sections.heading: Statutory illustrations
sections.body:
(a) Z is sitting in a moored boat on a river. A unfastens the moorings, and thus intentionally causes the boat to drift down the stream. Here A intentionally causes motion to Z, and he does this by disposing substances in such a manner that the motion is produced without any other action on any person’s part. A has therefore intentionally used force to Z; and if he has done so without Z’s consent, in order to the committing of any offence, or intending or knowing it to be likely that this use of force will cause injury, fear or annoyance to Z, A has used criminal force to Z
(b) Z is riding in a chariot. A lashes Z’s horses, and thereby causes them to quicken their pace. Here A has caused change of motion to Z by inducing the animals to change their motion. A has therefore used force to Z; and if A has done this without Z’s consent, intending or knowing it to be likely that he may thereby injure, frighten or annoy Z, A has used criminal force to Z
(c) Z is riding in a palanquin. A, intending to rob Z, seizes the pole and stops the palanquin. Here A has caused cessation of motion to Z, and he has done this by his own bodily power. A has therefore used force to Z; and as A has acted thus intentionally, without Z’s consent, in order to the commission of an offence. A has used criminal force to Z
(d) A intentionally pushes against Z in the street. Here A has by his own bodily power moved his own person so as to bring it into contact with Z. He has therefore intentionally used force to Z; and if he has done so without Z’s consent, intending or knowing it to be likely that he may thereby injure, frighten or annoy Z, he has used criminal force to Z
(e) A throws a stone, intending or knowing it to be likely that the stone will be thus brought into contact with Z, or with Z’s clothes, or with something carried by Z, or that it will strike water and dash up the water against Z’s clothes or something carried by Z. Here, if the throwing of the stone produce the effect of causing any substance to come into contact with Z, or Z’s clothes, A has used force to Z, and if he did so without Z’s consent, intending thereby to injure, frighten or annoy Z, he has used criminal force to Z
(f) A intentionally pulls up a woman’s veil. Here A intentionally uses force to her, and if he does so without her consent intending or knowing it to be likely that he may thereby injure, frighten or annoy her, he has used criminal force to her
(g) Z is bathing. A pours into the bath water which he knows to be boiling. Here A intentionally by his own bodily power causes such motion in the boiling water as brings that water into contact with Z, or with other water so situated that such contact must affect Z’s sense of feeling; A has therefore intentionally used force to Z; and if he has done this without Z’s consent intending or knowing it to be likely that he may thereby cause injury, fear or annoyance to Z, A has used criminal force
(h) A incites a dog to spring upon Z, without Z’s consent. Here, if A intends to cause injury, fear or annoyance to Z, he uses criminal force to Z

learningObjectives: Master the definition of criminal force under BNS s. 129.
Analyze the essential elements: intentional use of force, absence of victim's consent, and culpable purpose.
Examine the three alternative mental states: intending to commit an offence, or intending/knowing it likely to cause injury, fear, or annoyance.
Apply statutory illustrations of criminal force.
enhancement.definition: BNS s. 129 defines criminal force as intentionally using force to any person, without that person's consent, in order to the committing of any offence, or intending by the use of such force to cause, or knowing it to be likely that by the use of such force he will cause injury, fear or annoyance to the person to whom the force is used.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Criminalizes unauthorized non-consensual physical force applied with unlawful felonious intent or with the knowledge that it will cause injury, fear, or annoyance.
statutoryFramework: Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body, BNS s. 129 (corresponding to IPC s. 350).
Actus reus: Using force (as defined in s. 128) to another person without consent.
Mens rea 1: In order to the committing of any offence.
Mens rea 2: Intending or knowing it likely to cause injury, fear, or annoyance.
Statutory illustrations: Unmooring a boat to cause drifting; setting a dog on someone; pulling off a woman's veil.
essentialIngredients: The accused used force to another person within the meaning of Section 128.
The force was used WITHOUT the other person's consent.
The force was used to commit an offence; OR with intent/knowledge that it would cause injury, fear, or annoyance.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 129 transforms mechanical force (Section 128) into a criminal offence. Three prerequisites must coexist: (1) intentional application of force; (2) total absence of consent from the victim; and (3) one of two culpable mental states: either in order to commit a crime (e.g., snatching a purse or restraining an officer), or intending/knowing that the force will cause 'injury' (harm to body, mind, reputation, or property), 'fear' (apprehension of danger), or 'annoyance' (irritation or indignity). Classic statutory illustrations include tearing away a veil, spitting on someone, throwing water over someone, or inciting a dog to bark and leap at a pedestrian.
examples: Teaching example (Tearing off veil / scarf): An accused intentionally pulls off a woman's scarf in a public market without her consent, intending to humiliate and annoy her. This constitutes using criminal force under s. 129.

Teaching example (Setting a dog): An accused sics an aggressive bulldog on a mail carrier, causing the dog to spring forward. Even if the dog does not bite, the carrier is subjected to terror and forced motion, constituting criminal force.
distinctions: Criminal Force (s. 129) vs Hurt (s. 114): Criminal force is the physical act of non-consensual force causing fear, injury, or annoyance; Hurt requires proof of actual bodily pain, disease, or infirmity.
Criminal Force (s. 129) vs Assault (s. 130): Criminal force involves completed physical contact or altered motion; Assault is the preceding gesture or threat.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether an accused who threw a bucket of dirty water over a pedestrian's clothes to harass him used criminal force.
Rule: Causing a substance to come into contact with another person without consent intending to cause annoyance constitutes criminal force under BNS s. 129.
Application: Throwing water causes substance contact without consent, and intentional annoyance was evident.
Conclusion: The accused used criminal force under BNS s. 129.

shortAnswer: State BNS s. 129 definition and IPC s. 350 correspondence.
List key elements: force + absence of consent + intent to commit offence or cause injury/fear/annoyance.
Cite a standard statutory illustration (e.g., unmooring boat, pulling veil).
tenMark: Analysis of 'without consent' and the threshold of 'annoyance'.
Comparison with mechanical force (s. 128) and assault (s. 130).
sixteenMark: Comprehensive doctrinal analysis of criminal force in penal law.
Dissection of the mens rea alternatives: committing an offence vs injury/fear/annoyance.
The statutory illustrations of Section 129 and their modern digital/physical equivalents.
The role of consent and vitiation of consent under Section 24 BNS.

keyTakeaways: Converts physical force into an offence when used without consent.
Requires intent to commit an offence or cause injury, fear, or annoyance.
Includes non-injurious indignities like splashing water or pulling clothing.
Predicative basis for assault and criminal force charges (ss. 131-136).
